question: The Apollonio-Socrepes cableway in the province of Belluno is a public-private partnership (PPP) project1 forming part of the works for the Milan-Cortina 2026 Olympics. The project is located in P2-P3 risk area, of relevance under the Floods Directive,2 and has been issued a negative SEA opinion3 due to the risk of landslides and geological instability.

Nevertheless, the Veneto Regional Technical Committee approved the EIA,4provided that measures were taken to mitigate the hydro-geological risk. The matter is the subject of complaints, and in October the Lazio Regional Administrative Court will rule on an appeal on geological security and procedural issues.

The contracts for the works were awarded through a negotiated procedure after the failure of a public call for tenders, in which the lead operators did not participate owing to project design doubts and time constraints. This raises doubts over the project’s compliance with EU legislation,5 which only permits negotiated procedures in exceptional cases.
The Commission has already warned Italy over its excessive use of negotiated procedures6. In the light of the above: 1.
Is the project approval and implementation procedure in line with the SEA, EIA and Floods Directives, and with the precautionary principle?7
Do the approval procedure and the geological research and risk mitigation measures meet the EU minimum standards for EIAs?
Is the use of the negotiated procedure in line with that Directive and also consonant with the previous complaints lodged on that subject?

Proposal for a Public Private Partnership. Directive 2007/60/EC (Floods Directive) Directive 2001/42/EC (SEA Directive) Directive 2011/92/EU, as amended by Directive 2014/52/EU (EIA Directive). Directive 2014/24/EU on public procurement; Letters of formal notice of 2019 and 2022. Article 191 TFEU
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.11.2025) The Commission recalls that the precautionary principle informs the Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA)1 and Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA)2 Directives. The two Directives aim to ensure that the potential negative effects of plans, programmes and projects are assessed and adequately addressed and provide for public information and participation.

In addition, the EIA Directive also includes access to justice provisions. Without prejudice to the Commission’s role as guardian of the Treaties, the obligation to ensure compliance with EU law lies primarily with the administrative and judicial authorities of the Member States. The Commission notes that national judicial proceedings have been initiated on the matter in question.

The Commission also notes that Article 32 of Directive 2014/24/EU3 sets out the conditions for the use of the negotiated procedure without prior publication. However, the implementation of acts of EU law is in the first place the responsibility of the Member States, that shall provide remedies sufficient to ensure effective legal protection in the relevant fields4.

It is therefore for national courts and review bodies, as laid down under the Directives on remedies in public procurement5, to assess according to the legal and factual circumstances of each case, whether these requirements are met, and therefore whether contracting authorities and entities complied with their obligations under EU law.
